system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
user_prompt:
Here are examples of what I expect:

--- Example 1 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Michael Smith | Age/Sex: 32/M | Admission: 02/03/2026 | Discharge: 05/03/2026
C/O: Loose stools, vomiting, and abdominal cramps for 3 days.
History: Multiple episodes of watery diarrhea with nausea, repeated vomiting, generalised weakness, and abdominal cramps. No blood in stools. No recent travel.
Past History: Hypothyroidism (2 years).
Examination: Temp 99.8°F | Pulse 112 bpm | BP 100/70 mmHg | RR 20/min | SpO₂ 98%.
Investigations: CBC — mild leukocytosis. Serum Electrolytes — hyponatremia. Stool — no blood/parasites. RFT — mildly elevated creatinine due to dehydration.

Output:
Michael Smith, a 32-year-old man, was admitted on 02/03/2026 and discharged on 05/03/2026. He came with 3 days of loose motions (watery diarrhea), vomiting, stomach cramps, and weakness. He has had hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) for 2 years. On arrival, his temperature was 99.8°F (mild fever), pulse was 112 bpm (fast heart rate; normal is 60–100), blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg (borderline low; normal is 120/80), respiratory rate was 20/min, and oxygen was normal at 98%. Blood tests showed leukocytosis (mild rise in infection-fighting cells) and hyponatremia (low salt/sodium levels due to fluid loss). Stool tests showed no blood or parasites. Kidney tests showed mildly raised creatinine due to dehydration (lack of fluids). He was treated with IV fluids and supportive medicines, improved well, and was safely discharged home.

--- Example 2 ---
Original Medical Report:
Patient Name: Robert Brown | Age/Sex: 58/M | Admission: 25/03/2026 | Discharge: 30/03/2026
C/O: Chest pain and sweating for 6 hours.
History: Sudden onset retrosternal chest pain radiating to the left arm, sweating, mild breathlessness.
Past History: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (8 years). Hypertension (10 years). Dyslipidemia.
Examination: Temp 98.4°F | Pulse 96 bpm | BP 160/100 mmHg | RR 22/min | SpO₂ 95%.
Investigations: ECG — ST depression in anterior leads. Troponin-I — elevated. 2D Echo — mild left ventricular dysfunction. Lipid Profile — elevated LDL cholesterol.

Output:
Robert Brown, a 58-year-old man, was admitted on 25/03/2026 and discharged on 30/03/2026. He has an 8-year history of diabetes (sugar), 10-year hypertension (high BP), and dyslipidemia (high blood cholesterol). He arrived with 6 hours of sudden central chest pain spreading to his left arm, sweating, and mild breathlessness. His temperature was 98.4°F (normal), pulse was 96 bpm, blood pressure was high at 160/100 mmHg (normal 120/80), and oxygen saturation was 95% (borderline). An ECG and elevated troponin-I (a heart damage marker) confirmed a mild heart attack. A 2D Echo (heart ultrasound scan) showed mild left ventricular dysfunction (mild pumping weakness of the heart), and tests showed elevated bad LDL cholesterol. He was stabilized on heart medications and blood thinners, recovered safely, and was discharged home.

output_text:
You were diagnosed with sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis (lung TB) in 2019, and the disease was confirmed on 07/02/2020. You then developed pulmonary complications (lung problems) secondary to tuberculosis, including a spontaneous pneumothorax (collapsed lung) on the right side. On 03/02/2020 a right chest drainage (tube to remove air/fluid) was placed, followed by a pleurostomy (chest opening to drain fluid) on 03/03/2020. The pleurostomy was closed on 03/03/2020 because the lung collapsed, and a Heimlich valve (one‑way valve) was attached on 10/03 to allow air to escape. The Heimlich valve was removed on 27/03, but the drain was left open for the ostomy (continued drainage). A new pleurotomy (new chest opening) was done on 31/03. Because of bleeding inside tuberculous cavities (areas of dead tissue), an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (chest surgery to look inside) was performed on 07/04, and the cavity was packed (filled with compresses) to stop the bleeding. On 11/04/2020 a right pneumonectomy (removal of the right lung) was carried out by lateral thoracotomy (side chest incision) together with a tracheostomy (hole in the neck for a breathing tube). Both the chest drain and the tracheostomy tube were removed on 06/06.

During the stay you had three surgical wound infections caused by multidrug‑resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (hard‑to‑treat bacteria). You were treated with vancomycin (antibiotic to fight infection), meropenem (strong antibiotic), and amikacin (antibiotic), and this antibiotic therapy was stopped on 02/04 after you improved clinically and your procalcitonin (infection marker) fell to 0.09. You also experienced hypovolemic shock (low‑blood‑volume shock) due to surgical wound bleeding from the pleurostomy, which required urgent surgery on 07/04. On 10/04 you suffered a cardiopulmonary arrest (heart stopped) in asystole (no heartbeat) for about four minutes because of low oxygen (hypoxia).

You were admitted on 03/02/2020 and discharged on 09/05/2020 after a stay of three months, six days and seven hours in a ward bed, with the payer listed as SUS. [person] was referred to us because of a persistent dry cough for four weeks, night sweats, and a fever three days before admission that was not measured, along with shortness of breath (dyspnea). One day before admission you had sudden right‑side chest pain radiating to the right neck area, with worsening shortness of breath. You denied coughing up blood or sputum. You mentioned a weight loss of about eight kilograms one month ago, and you have been in prison for roughly three to six years without symptoms during that time. You have no urinary or bowel changes.

On examination you were pale (1/4), hydrated, not blue (acyanotic), not yellow (anictic), conscious and oriented. Your heart rate was 85 beats per minute with normal rhythmic sounds (normal S1 and S2) and no murmurs. Breathing sounds (vesicular breath sounds) were heard normally on the left side but were absent on the right side, with asymmetrical chest expansion and no extra sounds. Your oxygen saturation was 98%. The abdomen was flat with normal bowel sounds, soft and without signs of peritonitis. Your limbs showed no swelling (edema), no deep‑vein‑thrombosis signs, and good peripheral perfusion. The surgical wound was dry, with sutures intact and no opening (dehiscence).

A sensitivity test for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (TB bacteria) was done on sputum collected on 02/03/2020, processed on 28/02/2020, and released on the same day using DNA hybridisation (geno type mtbdr plus) which showed sensitivity to rifampin (drug) and isoniazid (drug). A bacilloscopy (Ziehl‑Neelsen stain) on sputum collected on 02/03/2020 and released on 02/07/2020 showed 10 to 99 acid‑fast bacilli (TB germs) per 100 fields.

Your follow‑up plan includes continuing the anti‑TB regimen (RI) for two more months, taking oral iron replacement (iron supplement) as prescribed, and attending the scheduled follow‑up appointments at [organization] with the thoracic surgery team. A meeting was held with [person] together with the thoracic surgery team, during which the condition and treatment were explained, and [person] understood the guidelines and appreciated the care. You were instructed about warning signs and told to call if any concerns arise. A report and contact details for assisted treatment were provided by the infectious diseases and thoracic surgery services. At discharge you were in good general condition with no complaints.
